ver+ EducationChocó · ColombiaData as of 27 Sep 2026

Chocó's education system, on a map

A first look at the department's 1,271 public school sites: where they are, how many students they serve and how they fared after the 10 August 2026 earthquake. Damage comes from the Chocó Education Authority's 29 September report and, for Quibdó, from the MEN layer. Each dot is a school site. Click any dot to see its details.

Quick read

Six features of the system

  • 89%Rural and scattered. 1,127 of the 1,271 school sites are rural. Half have 31 students or fewer, and 6 in 10 have fewer than 50.
  • 146,975Students in public schools. 56% study in rural areas. Quibdó alone has 22% of the enrolment.
  • 647School sites damaged by the earthquake (51%), 172 of them with critical damage. 295 school sites with 62,030 students had suspended operations.
  • ≈ 6 hFar from everything. The typical school site is about 6 hours from the nearest city. Across most of the territory, access is by river.
  • 95%Few partners. 618 of the 647 damaged school sites had no prior private partner on the ground.
  • 42%PDET territory. 530 school sites are in PDET (post-conflict priority municipalities), prioritised for reconstruction after the armed conflict.

How to read it

What the map shows and what it does not

Location accuracy

    Satellite imagery

    • The background is the 2024 cloud-free Sentinel‑2 mosaic (10 m per pixel), from the European Space Agency (Copernicus), processed by EOX. Chocó is one of the cloudiest places on Earth, so this is a composite of many passes, not a photo from a single day.
    • The whole department is shown at medium resolution. When you zoom in on Quibdó or Istmina, the map loads the full 10 m resolution.
    • Building damage comes from Copernicus EMS (activation EMSR916). It was identified by visual interpretation of Pléiades Neo (0.3 m) and SkySat (0.5 m) images from 13 August 2026. It covers only central Quibdó and the urban area of Istmina. Outside those areas there is no satellite damage assessment.
    • For each school site with its own coordinate, the details panel shows how many damaged buildings Copernicus found within 300 m. It is a warning sign to visit the school, not an assessment of the school itself.

    Population, travel time and night lights

    • Population aged 5 to 19: WorldPop 2025 (R2025A, 100 m, constrained to built-up areas), adding the 5–9, 10–14 and 15–19 age groups. For Chocó this gives about 153,000 children and young people. It is a statistical model, not a census.
    • More than 3 km from a school: straight-line distance from each populated cell to the nearest school site with coordinates. Because 708 school sites have no coordinate of their own, the figure overstates the gap. Juradó (99.7%) and Unión Panamericana (96.7%) are almost certainly a coordinate problem. Use it to decide where to check on the ground.
    • Travel time: Malaria Atlas Project (2015). The median school site with coordinates is about 6 hours from the nearest city of more than 50,000 people, and 549 school sites are more than 6 hours away. The model handles rivers only roughly, so in Chocó it is a measure of remoteness, not a boat travel time.
    • Mobile coverage: MinTIC reports, by operator, which technologies reach each village. The latest published cut for Chocó is 2023 Q3. The map places DANE's 401 villages (DIVIPOLA); those missing from the report are shown as "no coverage reported". A village with 4G does not guarantee signal at the school, which may sit on the outskirts. Each school card uses the nearest village within 3 km.
    • Night lights: NASA VIIRS, 20 Sep 2026. It shows where there is steady lighting. At this resolution it cannot measure power cuts caused by the earthquake.

    Access

    • The road network comes from OpenStreetMap. In Chocó it may be incomplete, especially for rural paths and tracks, which are not included.
    • Rivers are the main way to reach most rural school sites. The map does not measure travel times or costs. That layer should be built with the field team.
    • Each details panel has links to Google Maps (location, satellite view and directions). Google only calculates routes by land, so for most rural school sites it does not reflect real access by river.
    • Nuevo Belén de Bajirá was created in 2022 and has no boundary of its own in the maps used. Its school sites appear inside Riosucio and Carmen del Darién.

    Sources: MEN, layer «Sedes educativas afectadas por el sismo del 2026-08-10» (ArcGIS, MEN_1700_00) · MEN, DANE-SISE school site directory (2025-12) · ExE, Un millón de razones dashboard (prior private partners, % of enrolment affected) · DANE (IPM 2018) · MEN (net enrolment 2024) · ICFES (Saber 11 2022) · © OpenStreetMap contributors (roads, rivers and airfields, ODbL), accessed 27 Sep 2026 · Sentinel‑2 cloudless 2024, s2maps.eu, by EOX IT Services GmbH (contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2024, CC BY‑NC‑SA 4.0) · Copernicus Emergency Management Service, EMSR916 AOI04 and AOI05 (© European Union, 2026) · WorldPop (2025), Global2 R2025A, CC BY 4.0 · Malaria Atlas Project, Accessibility to Cities 2015 and Walking-only Travel Time to Healthcare 2020 (Weiss et al.), CC BY 4.0 · NASA Black Marble / GIBS, VIIRS NOAA‑20 · MinTIC, Cobertura móvil por tecnología, departamento y municipio por proveedor (datos.gov.co 9mey-c8s8) · DANE, DIVIPOLA villages (xaxy-8nri)· Municipal boundaries: maps from the ExE dashboard.
